description: "Intended," as its Dedication states, "as an initiatory suggestion for popularizing some of the characteristics of American Landscape and American Art," this historically significant book shows how art, patriotism, and spirituality were woven together to confer a distinctive and hallowed identity on places of natural beauty in mid-nineteenth-century America, decisively influencing the development of the conservation movement. The book contains a richly heterogeneous collection of essays on nature and art, culture and character, often harmoniously mingling certain subjects--such as natural beauty and the glories of technology--which later generations have assumed to be unrelated or even opposed, and repeatedly sounding themes that resonate throughout the cultural history of American conservationism: wild nature as a source of moral, spiritual and patriotic inspiration (Magoon's essay); the spiritual superiority of American over European scenery (Cooper); the coming ascendance of the suburban ideal (Willis); the beauties of a railroad in the beauties of its landscape (Taylor). The distinction of some of the book's literary contributors is matched by the importance of its illustrations: engravings of works by major American landscape artists such as Frederic Edwin Church, Thomas Cole, John Frederick Kensett, Jasper F. Cropsey, and Asher B. Durand, men who helped to define a particularly American aesthetic of nature from which preservationist conservationism arose as both moral response and commercial opportunity. These illustrations invoke the power of that artistic tradition, even as they draw their inspiration from the Arcadian East which antedated the wilderness West as the nation's first landscape ideal. Like so much of American conservationism itself, moreover, this volume owes its historic character to a blend of idealistic values and business enterprise: it was one of the first to define and exploit the market for sumptuous images of native scenery in elegant and accessible presentation-book form, a prototype of all the coffee-table tomes that have made images of the nation's natural beauties a patriotic accessory in the ordinary American home.
